questions.problem:
Find the sum modulo $18$ of the solutions to the congruence $8x≡14\,(\text{mod}\,18).$

*Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.*
questions.worked_solution:
In the given congruence, we have $a=8$ and $n=18$, and so 

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(8,18)=2.
$$

Since $b=14$ is divisible by $2,$ our congruence has $2$ solutions.

First, we use the division property of congruences:

$$
\begin{aligned}8x & ≡14 &  & (\text{mod}\,18) \\ 2\cdot 4x & ≡2\cdot 7 &  & (\text{mod}\,2\cdot 9) \\ \cancel{2}\cdot 4x & ≡\cancel{2}\cdot 7 &  & (\text{mod}\,\cancel{2}\cdot 9) \\ 4x & ≡7 &  & (\text{mod}\,9)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in this new congruence, we have ${a}_{1}=4$ and ${n}_{1}=9$, where

$$
\text{gcd}({a}_{1},{n}_{1})=\text{gcd}(4,9)=1.
$$

So, our congruence has a unique solution modulo $9.$

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $4\,(\text{mod}\,9).$ To find the inverse of $4\,(\text{mod}\,9),$ we compute the exponents of $4\,(\text{mod}\,9)$ until we get a result of $1\,(\text{mod}\,9):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{2} & ≡16≡9+7≡7 &  & (\text{mod}\,9) \\ {4}^{3} & ≡7\cdot 4≡28≡3\cdot 9+1≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,9)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $4\cdot 7≡1\,(\text{mod}\,9),$ which means that $7$ is the multiplicative inverse of $4$ (modulo $9$). 

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & ≡7 &  & (\text{mod}\,9) \\ 7\cdot 4x & ≡7\cdot 7 &  & (\text{mod}\,9) \\ (7\cdot 4)x & ≡49 &  & (\text{mod}\,9) \\ x & ≡49 &  & (\text{mod}\,9) \\ x & ≡5\cdot 9+4 &  & (\text{mod}\,9) \\ x & ≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,9)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the solution $x≡4\,(\text{mod}\,9).$ 

But our original congruence was modulo $18$ (not modulo $9$). To find all the solutions modulo $18,$ we repeatedly add $9$ modulo $18$ until we reach the number $4$ again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,18) \\ {x}_{2} & ≡4+9≡13 &  & (\text{mod}\,18) \\ {x}_{3} & ≡13+9≡22≡1\cdot 18+4≡4≡{x}_{1} &  & (\text{mod}\,18)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x≡4,13\,(\text{mod}\,18).$ 

Finally,

$$
4+13≡17\,(\text{mod}\,18).
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following congruences have *precisely two* solutions modulo $16?$

I. $6x \equiv 14 \quad (\text{mod}\:16)$

II. $4x \equiv 8 \quad (\text{mod}\:16)$

III. $2x \equiv 9 \quad (\text{mod}\:16)$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14269988/assets/b65fc4830e0b060d62226b41d5ccb7bdc63d0ad594f7a42a2628597409bba3af.png)

      

Recall the following facts regarding the congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n){:}$

- The congruence has no solutions modulo $n$ if and only if 

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n) \!\not{|}\:b.
$$

- The congruence has $\textrm{gcd}(a,n)$ solutions modulo $n$ if and only if 

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n) \:{|}\:b.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our congruences.

- Congruence I has two solutions modulo $16.$ We have $a=6$ and $n=16,$ and

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(6,16)=2.
$$

Since $b=14$ is divisible by $2,$ this congruence has $2$ solutions.

- Congruence II has four solutions modulo $16.$ We have $a=4$ and $n=16,$ and

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(4,16)=4.
$$

Since $b=8$ is divisible by $4,$ this congruence has $4$ solutions.

- Congruence III has no solutions. We have $a=2$ and $n=16,$ and

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(2,16)=2.
$$

Since $b=9$ is not divisible by $2,$ this congruence has no solutions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the sum modulo $20$ of the solutions to the congruence $8x \equiv 4 \:(\text{mod}\:20).$ 

*Hint: You may wish to use trial and error to find the appropriate multiplicative inverse.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In the given congruence, we have $a=8$ and $n=20,$ so

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(8,20)=4.
$$

Since $b=4$ is divisible by $4,$ our congruence has $4$ solutions.

First, we reduce the congruence using the division property of congruences:

$$
\begin{aligned}8x & ≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ 4\cdot 2x & ≡4\cdot 1 &  & (\text{mod}\,4\cdot 5) \\ \cancel{4}\cdot 2x & ≡\cancel{4}\cdot 1 &  & (\text{mod}\,\cancel{4}\cdot 5) \\ 2x & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in the new congruence, we have $a_1=2$ and $n_1=5,$ so

$$
\text{gcd}(a_1,n_1)=\text{gcd}(2,5)=1.
$$

This means our congruence has a unique solution modulo $5.$

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $2\,(\textrm{mod}\:5).$ To find the inverse of $2\,(\textrm{mod}\:5),$ we compute the exponents of $2\,(\textrm{mod}\:5)$ until we get a result of $1 \,(\textrm{mod}\:5)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2} & ≡4 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ {2}^{3} & ≡4\cdot 2≡8≡1\cdot 5+3≡3 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ {2}^{4} & ≡3\cdot 2≡6≡1\cdot 5+1≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $2 \cdot 3 \equiv 1 \:(\textrm{mod}\:5),$ which means that $3$ is the multiplicative inverse of $2$ (modulo $5$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our congruence by $3,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ 3\cdot 2x & ≡3\cdot 1 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ (3\cdot 2)x & ≡3 &  & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & ≡3 &  & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get one solution, $x \equiv 3 \: (\text{mod}\:5).$ 

But our original congruence was modulo $20$ (not modulo $5$). To find all the solutions modulo $20,$ we repeatedly add $5$ modulo $20$ until we reach the number $3$ again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ≡3 &  & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ {x}_{2} & ≡3+5≡8 &  & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ {x}_{3} & ≡8+5≡13 &  & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ {x}_{4} & ≡13+5≡18 &  & (\text{mod}\,20) \\ {x}_{5} & ≡18+5≡23≡1\cdot 20+3≡3≡{x}_{1} &  & (\text{mod}\,20)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x\equiv 3, 8, 13, 18 \: (\text{mod}\:20).$ 

Finally,

$$
3+8+13+18 \equiv 2 \quad (\text{mod}\:20).
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

tutorials.name: Determining the Number of Solutions of a Linear Congruence
tutorials.problem:
The number of solutions to a modular equation

$$
ax \equiv  b \qquad (\text{mod}\:n)
$$

all depends on $\textrm{gcd}(a,n)\mathbin{:}$

- If $\textrm{gcd}(a,n) \not\mid b,$ then the congruence has no
solutions.

- If $\textrm{gcd}(a,n) \: | \:b,$  then the congruence has exactly $\textrm{gcd}(a,n)$ solutions in the interval $0 \leq x \leq n-1.$

We can summarize these rules using a flow chart, as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14269988/assets/b65fc4830e0b060d62226b41d5ccb7bdc63d0ad594f7a42a2628597409bba3af.png)

      

For example, consider the linear congruence

$$
6x \equiv 9 \qquad (\text{mod}\:15).
$$

In this congruence, we have $a=6$ and $n=15,$ and their greatest common divisor is

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(6,15)=3.
$$

Since $b=9$ is also divisible by $3,$ we conclude that our congruence has $3$ solutions in the interval $0 \leq x \leq 14.$ 

We can easily verify that the three solutions are $4, 9,$ and $14\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}6\cdot 4 & ≡24≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,15) &  & ✓ \\ 6\cdot 9 & ≡54≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,15) &  & ✓ \\ 6\cdot 14 & ≡84≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,15) &  & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}6\cdot 4 & ≡24≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,15) &  & ✓ \\ 6\cdot 9 & ≡54≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,15) &  & ✓ \\ 6\cdot 14 & ≡84≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,15) &  & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Solving Linear Congruences Using the Division Property
tutorials.problem:
Consider the following congruence:

$$
ax \equiv b \qquad (\text{mod}\:n)
$$

In cases where $\textrm{gcd}(a,n) > 1$ and $\textrm{gcd}(a,n) \mid b,$ it's possible to reduce the congruence to a simpler congruence with a unique solution. However, the solution to the simpler congruence is only *part* of the solution to the original congruence. An extra step is needed to find the complete solution. 

To demonstrate, let's find all the solutions to the following congruence: 

$$
2x \equiv 6 \qquad (\text{mod}\:10)
$$

Here, we have $a=2$ and $n=10,$ so

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(2,10)=2.
$$

Since $b=6$ is divisible by $2,$ our congruence has $2$ solutions modulo $10.$ 

Notice that we can simplify the congruence using the division property of congruences:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14269988/assets/def91d646b8c725e09b0d6f730e9b42c3c3ff5f3d93ca3bfef05357f581b1c01.svg)

Thus, our simplified congruence has the unique solution, $x \equiv {\color{blue}3} \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{red}5}).$ 

But remember, we expect $2$ solutions modulo $10.$ To find all the solutions, we repeatedly add the reduced modulus (${\color{red}5}$) to our reduced solution (${\color{blue}3}$) modulo $10$ until we reach our reduced solution (${\color{blue}3}$) again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ≡3 &  & (\text{mod}\,10) \\ {x}_{2} & ≡3+5≡8 &  & (\text{mod}\,10) \\ {x}_{3} & ≡8+5≡13≡10+3≡3 &  & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x\equiv {\color{blue}3} \: (\text{mod}\:10)$ and $x\equiv {\color{purple}{8}} \: (\text{mod}\:10).$

tutorials.title: Solving Linear Congruences Using the Division Property
tutorials.content:
Consider the following congruence:

$$
ax \equiv b \qquad (\text{mod}\:n)
$$

In cases where $\textrm{gcd}(a,n) > 1$ and $\textrm{gcd}(a,n) \mid b,$ it's possible to reduce the congruence to a simpler congruence with a unique solution. However, the solution to the simpler congruence is only *part* of the solution to the original congruence. An extra step is needed to find the complete solution. 

To demonstrate, let's find all the solutions to the following congruence: 

$$
2x \equiv 6 \qquad (\text{mod}\:10)
$$

Here, we have $a=2$ and $n=10,$ so

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(2,10)=2.
$$

Since $b=6$ is divisible by $2,$ our congruence has $2$ solutions modulo $10.$ 

Notice that we can simplify the congruence using the division property of congruences:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14269988/assets/def91d646b8c725e09b0d6f730e9b42c3c3ff5f3d93ca3bfef05357f581b1c01.svg)

Thus, our simplified congruence has the unique solution, $x \equiv {\color{blue}3} \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{red}5}).$ 

But remember, we expect $2$ solutions modulo $10.$ To find all the solutions, we repeatedly add the reduced modulus (${\color{red}5}$) to our reduced solution (${\color{blue}3}$) modulo $10$ until we reach our reduced solution (${\color{blue}3}$) again:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ≡3 &  & (\text{mod}\,10) \\ {x}_{2} & ≡3+5≡8 &  & (\text{mod}\,10) \\ {x}_{3} & ≡8+5≡13≡10+3≡3 &  & (\text{mod}\,10)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x\equiv {\color{blue}3} \: (\text{mod}\:10)$ and $x\equiv {\color{purple}{8}} \: (\text{mod}\:10).$
